items.body:
**Repository:** `openai/codex`
**Labels suggested:** `bug`, `platform:windows`, `perf:memory`, `area:desktop`
**Date filed:** 2026-10-22 (Asia/Shanghai)

---

## TL;DR

The Windows Store (MSIX) build of the Codex desktop app exhausts **nonpaged kernel pool**, not application memory. On the machine below it grows at a **steady 150–212 MB/min** while the app runs and stops **completely** the moment the app is closed. A 32 GB machine becomes unusable in roughly two hours; only a reboot returns the memory.

The leak is **not in Codex code**. It happens inside `bindflt.sys`, the Windows driver that implements MSIX AppData virtualisation, and it is triggered by opening a path that passes through a **junction under `%APPDATA%` / `%LOCALAPPDATA%`**. The same defect has already been independently diagnosed for another vendor's MSIX desktop app (`anthropics/claude-code#96870`). Both products are affected because both ship a Chromium-based desktop app inside an MSIX package.

This report contains a **causal confirmation, not just a correlation**: converting the two offending junctions back into plain directories drops the growth rate from ~150 MB/min to **below zero** on the same machine, same app, same session.

We are filing with Codex because **the packaging choice is the exposure vector**: any Codex user who moves their AppData to another volume — a common way to save space on small system drives — will hit this.

---

## Environment

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| OS | Windows 11 Home (Chinese), build `10.0.26200.9711` |
| Hardware | Laptop, 32 GB LPDDR5X (31.43 GB visible to the OS) |
| Package | `OpenAI.Codex_26.1016.6573.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0`, `SignatureKind=Store`, x64 |
| Executable | `ChatGPT.exe` 155.0.8059.80 (Electron / Chromium) |
| Package install volume | Not the system volume (junction from `C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\...` to another drive) |
| Relevant filter drivers | `bindflt` (Running / Auto), `FLTMGR`, `Ntfs`, plus an EFS filter on the target volume |
| Symbol decoding | `xperf -a pool -stacks` with an empty `_NT_SYMBOL_PATH` (module names only) |

---

## Impact

- Nonpaged pool reached **20.78 GB** after ~6 hours of uptime with the app running. At that point the system reported 96 % memory in use and 1.19 GB free.
- The arithmetic closes: 20.78 GB nonpaged pool + 7.88 GB total process working set + 1.07 GB paged pool ≈ 29.7 GB ≈ 30.18 GB in use. **No single user process was large.** The largest process working set on the whole machine was under 1 GB.
- The leak is only reclaimed by a reboot. Closing the app stops the growth but does not return the memory — the affected pages stay allocated in the pool.

---

## Evidence

### 1. A/B test: app present vs. absent

Nonpaged pool sampled with `Win32_PerfRawData_PerfOS_Memory.PoolNonpagedBytes`.

| Period | `ChatGPT.exe` processes | Nonpaged pool rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 240 s, app closed | **0** | **25 KB/min ≈ 0.0 MB/min** |
| 180 s, app running (fresh start) | **9** | **211.9 MB/min** |
| Steady state, app running | 8–9 | ~150 MB/min |

Absolute values: 10.01 GB → 10.06 GB over 5 minutes (app absent), then 10.06 GB → 10.68 GB over 3 minutes (app running).

The same machine ran a **competing Electron/Chromium application for the entire absent window with zero pool movement**. That rules out "Chromium" and "Electron" as the cause and points at the MSIX package identity.

### 2. Causal confirmation: removing the junctions eliminates the leak

**[Added 2026-10-22 20:00 UTC+8 — this is the decisive test]**

The two junctions on the app's hot path were converted back into plain directories by copying the data back to the system volume and deleting the reparse points. Nothing else changed: same package, same `ChatGPT.exe` build, same 9 processes, same session, no reboot.

| Condition | Junctions on hot path | Nonpaged pool rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline, before the change | 2 | ~150 MB/min |
| With `--disable-gpu-shader-disk-cache` | 2 | 171.3 MB/min |
| Fresh app start | 2 | 211.9 MB/min |
| **After junction → real directory** | **0** | **−2.2 MB/min (flat)** |

The post-change measurement is 16 samples over 457 seconds: 16.596 GB → 16.580 GB, i.e. **no growth at all** (the small negative delta is ordinary pool churn). Same app, still running with all 9 processes alive, still actively writing to the very same directories (206 files written within 3 minutes in one of them).

One additional junction (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex`, the CLI components directory) was **left untouched** during this test, and the leak still went to zero. So the trigger is not "any junction" — it is specifically the AppData junctions that the **desktop app itself reads and writes continuously**. That refines the original trigger description and matters for the fix: only the app's own data directory needs to be reparse-point-free.

**Limits of this test, stated plainly:** one continuous 7.6-minute window, same boot session, no reboot; the `NtFC` tag itself was not re-sampled with poolmon/xperf after the change (only the pool total, which is what the user experiences). It establishes the mechanism on this machine; it is not a long-duration study.

### 3. Pool tag breakdown (`xperf -a pool`, 60 s window)

Baseline 3.930 GB → 4.029 GB during the window. Nonpaged (`NX`) total 56,968.8 KB outstanding.

| Tag | Outstanding | Share of top 80 | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`NtFC`** | **40,150.5 KB** | **70.7 %** | NTFS file control blocks. 198,280 allocations, only 119 KB freed. |
| `smNp` / `smCB` / `smBt` | 9,892 KB | 17.4 % | ESENT database engine |
| `bfRH` | 4,212 KB | 7.4 % | BitLocker FVE (also appears in paged pool) |
| `FVEp` | 1,088 KB | 1.9 % | BitLocker FVE |
| `FMfn` | 485 KB | 0.9 % | Filter Manager |
| `File` / `Irp` / `Mdl` | 767 KB | 1.3 % | Generic |

Paged pool over the same window was only 8,521 KB — three orders of magnitude smaller than the leak.

### 4. Allocation stacks (`xperf -a pool -stacks`, 60 s window, 56,968.8 KB outstanding, 65 stack blocks)

**A single stack block accounts for 53,405.0 KB = 93.7 % of everything not freed, with 208,248 unfreed allocations.**

Top-down chain:

```
chrome.dll ×17
  → KernelBase ×2
    → ntdll
      → ntoskrnl
        → bindflt.sys ×2          ← MSIX AppData virtualisation
          → FLTMGR.SYS ×7         ← Filter Manager
            → Ntfs.sys ×3         ← allocates the NtFC block
              → ntoskrnl
```

`filecrypt.sys` (EFS) and `fvevol.sys` (BitLocker) also appear repeatedly on the same path.

### 5. Exclusions (each experimentally verified, not assumed)

| Hypothesis | Test | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SteelSeries GG (a background app) | Killed 7 processes, removed its `HKLM\...\Run` entry | 181 MB/min vs 188 MB/min before — unchanged |
| Windows Search indexer | `Stop-Service WSearch -Force`, confirmed indexer gone | 134.6 vs 137.9 MB/min — unchanged |
| Windows Defender | Checked protection state | Real-time protection off, service `Stopped/Manual` |
| Handle leak | 40 s sample | Pool +98 MB while `System` handles **−272** and total handles **−5,163** |
| GPU VRAM / TDR | Adapter counters, event log | Static; no TDR or display driver errors |
| Pagefile | Commit vs. physical | Not physical memory |
| A third-party AV filter driver | Present on the box | Only ~11 % on an independent stack shape |
| Chromium / Electron in general | Ran another Electron app throughout | Zero growth |
| Codex CLI | Separate Win32 binary, ran normally | Zero growth |

---

## Root cause

`NtFC` blocks come from `Ntfs.sys`. Stack block #2 above shows they are allocated while the request passes through `bindflt.sys`, and only when the app is running inside its MSIX package context. Method-level analysis of the same defect in another MSIX desktop app (`anthropics/claude-code#96870`) identifies the exact mechanism, and our trace is consistent with it:

1. `bindflt.sys` registers an `IRP_MJ_CREATE` pre-operation callback. To decide whether a path needs AppData remapping it **probes the path by opening it itself**, with `FltCreateFileEx2(FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES, FILE_OPEN, IO_STOP_ON_SYMLINK)`.
2. `IO_STOP_ON_SYMLINK` means "do not follow a reparse point; stop and hand me the target". When the probe hits a **junction**, NTFS returns `STATUS_STOPPED_ON_SYMLINK` together with a `REPARSE_DATA_BUFFER` that NTFS allocated in nonpaged pool (tag `NtFC`).
3. One code path in the callback (the redirect path) correctly hands that buffer onward as `TagData` with `STATUS_REPARSE`, and `IopParseDevice` frees it.
4. **The probe path returns success without freeing the buffer.** The allocation is orphaned. It is never reclaimed — not on handle close, not on process exit, not when the junction is deleted. Only a reboot clears it.

Per-open cost is about **272 bytes (one `NtFC` block)**. The observed 211.9 MB/min therefore corresponds to roughly 780,000 opens per minute, i.e. about 13,000 file opens per second — entirely plausible for a Chromium renderer that continuously touches Preferences, Local Storage, IndexedDB metadata and cache indexes under `%APPDATA%`.

### Why this machine hits it hard

`%APPDATA%\Roaming\Codex` and `%APPDATA%\Local\Codex` in this installation are **junctions** pointing to another volume (the user relocated AppData to free space on the system drive). That turns an ordinary directory lookup into a reparse-point stop on the hottest path in the application, tens of thousands of times per second.

The general form of the trigger is documented in the sibling report: **an MSIX desktop app + a junction anywhere under `%APPDATA%` / `%LOCALAPPDATA%` that the app keeps touching**. Common ways users create such junctions without knowing:

- Relocating app data to another drive to save system-drive space (this case).
- `uv`-managed Python minor-version junctions under `%APPDATA%\uv\python\...`.
- `nvm-windows` `.nodejs` junction on `PATH`.
- `pnpm` global symlink farms under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\pnpm`.
- Any tool that "moves" a user profile folder and leaves a reparse point behind.

---

## Known workarounds, and what does not work

**[Added 2026-10-22 — measured on the reporting machine]**

**Does not work here: `--disable-gpu-shader-disk-cache`.** This flag is reported as effective by other users (see `openai/codex#44271` comment by KarlAvec1K and `#44995` comment by firxyqwer-star). On this machine it was passed to the app through `IApplicationActivationManager::ActivateApplication` so that MSIX package identity was preserved (confirmed: the main process command line contained the flag), and the measured rate was **171.3 MB/min over 421 seconds** — the same order as the no-flag baseline. It suppressed nothing here. Most likely the shader cache is only one of several writers on the hot path in this installation, so blocking that one leaves the rest untouched. Worth knowing before suggesting it as the fix.

**Works here: make the app's data directories real directories.** Converting `%APPDATA%\Roaming\Codex` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Codex` from junctions into plain directories (data copied back to the system volume) dropped the rate to zero — see section 2 above. Cost is disk space on the system volume; nothing else changed.

**Works here: use the Codex CLI instead of the desktop app.** `codex.exe` is a plain Win32 binary, does not run under MSIX package identity, and never enters `bindflt`'s virtualisation path. Measured pool growth while it ran: **0**.

**Interim mitigation:** close the app when idle, or reboot every ~2 hours. Follow `(Get-CimInstance Win32_PerfRawData_PerfOS_Memory).PoolNonpagedBytes / 1GB` to know where you stand.

---

## What we are asking for

We are **not** asking Codex to work around a Windows kernel defect, and we understand the actual fix belongs with the OS vendor. Concretely:

1. **Track this as a known Windows issue** in the Codex packaging / distribution area, so support and triage can recognise it instead of chasing "Codex uses too much memory".
2. **Document the trigger, now that it is verified.** A short note would do: *"If `%APPDATA%\Roaming\Codex` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Codex` is a junction or symlink (for example because you moved app data to another drive), long-running sessions can exhaust kernel nonpaged pool. Keep them as real directories, or accept that the app must be restarted periodically."* Measured effect of following this: leak goes to zero.
3. **Offer or document a non-MSIX Windows install path.** The MSIX packaging is what places every file operation behind `bindflt`. A Win32 installer (or the CLI as the recommended Windows path) removes the exposure surface entirely.
4. **Avoid needing a junction for the data directory in the first place**: honour an environment variable or config key that relocates user data without a reparse point, mirroring what the CLI already does via `CODEX_HOME`. Users who relocate data today end up with a junction whether they intended one or not.
5. If your telemetry can distinguish pool pressure from working-set pressure, this failure mode would have surfaced long ago — worth considering for future Windows builds.

---

## Related reports

**Same defect, other MSIX apps**

- `anthropics/claude-code#96870` — traces it to `bindflt.sys` with method-level detail. Open as of 2026-10-22.
- `anthropics/claude-code#95489` — `NtFC` leak at ~230 MB/min, very close to the 211.9 MB/min measured here.
- `anthropics/claude-code#96722`, `#94198`, `#91265` — related kernel pool growth in the same package model.
- `anthropics/claude-code#94454`, `#92779` — `bindflt.sys` crash variants (`PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA`, `STOP 0x50`), i.e. the same driver's failure modes are not limited to leaking.

**Earlier Codex reports that did not reach the kernel layer**

- `openai/codex#55812` (2026-10-21) — "Severe Kernel Nonpaged Pool Memory Leak (Tag: NtFc) triggered by Codex Desktop".
- `openai/codex#44995` (2026-09-12) — `NtFC` grows while Codex is open; includes the `--disable-gpu-shader-disk-cache` A/B.
- `openai/codex#44271` (2026-09-09) — Windows Codex work causes `NtFC` pool leak and RAM exhaustion; includes an independent A/B of the same flag.
- `openai/codex#26015`, `#38059` — earlier memory complaints, attributed to application memory at the time.

**Microsoft**

- Feedback Hub item filed by the sibling report's author: https://aka.ms/AA13ld3q
- A separate report naming `bindflt.sys` directly has been written for the Windows kernel team.

---

## Desensitisation note

This report contains no username, machine name, account identifier, credential, or e-mail address. Volume letters are generic; package and version strings are public.

items.body:
## Summary

In Codex desktop chats connected to a Linux host over SSH, `attach_artifact`, `attach_worktree`, and `create_worktree` can remain pending until the user interrupts the turn. Correlating the retained desktop logs with remote rollout records for October 22, 2026 shows a consistent distinction: all six calls on queued turns lacked a logged response, while all ten calls on directly submitted turns returned.

Read-only inspection and an isolated reproduction using the installed renderer's relevant functions suggest that inferred turn parameters lack `clientUserMessageId`, causing a message-ownership check to return without executing or responding to the dynamic tool request.

## Environment

- macOS 26.2, build 25C56.
- Desktop application version 26.1013.31256, build 20586, production channel.
- Desktop build commit recorded in logs: `f07f286327f3c9ef2b2f799b64b0393fdc1bdeed`.
- Remote Linux execution over SSH; affected requests arrive through `item/tool/call`.
- The app update check returned `busy`, so this report does not claim reproduction on the latest available release.

## Observed reproduction sequence

1. Open a Codex chat connected to a remote Linux repository over SSH.
2. While a turn is running, queue a follow-up that will need an app tool such as creating a managed worktree or attaching a PR.
3. Let the queued follow-up start after the current turn finishes.
4. The app tool remains pending. The remote rollout identifies the turn trigger as `queue`.
5. Interrupt the stuck turn and submit a follow-up directly after the chat becomes idle. Directly submitted turns provided the successful comparison cases in the retained logs.

These steps describe the observed workflow; a new controlled end-to-end reproduction was not performed.

## Actual behavior and evidence

| Remote turn trigger | Calls examined | Tool response logged | No tool response logged |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `composer` | 10 | 10 | 0 |
| `queue` | 6 | 0 | 6 |

All six unresolved requests reached the Mac and logged both `dynamic_app_tool_server_request_received` and `dynamic_app_tool_renderer_execution_started`. None logged `Sending server response` for the matching call ID. The renderer-start marker precedes the ownership check; it does not establish that the tool operation actually ran.

A representative `create_worktree` request was received at `2026-10-22T11:36:22.471Z`, entered the renderer dispatcher at `11:36:22.495Z`, and remained pending until interruption at `11:54:39.106Z`. The turn was queue-triggered and its persisted opening user-message item had a non-null client ID.

A successful attachment at `06:30:43Z` logged `thread/attachment/add`, `thread/attachment/list`, and a tool response. An attachment to the same PR at `06:45:01Z`, on a queued turn, logged only the dispatcher markers and remained pending until interruption.

## Suspected cause and offline validation

The installed renderer contains the following path:

1. `turn/started` creates a missing turn using inferred parameters that omit `clientUserMessageId`.
2. The ordinary opening user-message handler stores the incoming item, including its `clientId`, without filling that parameter.
3. The dynamic tool dispatcher rejects a non-null message `clientId` that differs from the turn's `clientUserMessageId`, including when the latter is absent.
4. This branch returns `false` before claiming execution or loading the tool implementation. Its caller discards the return value, leaving the request without an error or success response.

An offline harness using those installed function bodies and dependency stubs reproduced the early return. Supplying the matching turn parameter passed the guard and reached an execution-claim sentinel. No app tool was executed, and no running application files were changed.

Historical renderer heap state was not captured, and the harness is not a full end-to-end test. The queue correlation and code-path reproduction strongly support this explanation, but do not prove the exact in-memory values in every failed call.

## Expected behavior and suggested investigation

Queued turns should retain the authoritative opening message identity so valid app tools execute exactly once. Please investigate synchronization of message identity in inferred turns while preserving multi-client ownership checks. An unhandled request should receive an actionable failure or be routed to a legitimate owner rather than wait indefinitely. Log ownership rejections and cover queued SSH turns in regression tests.

## Workaround

Wait for the preceding turn to finish before directly submitting a request that needs these app tools. For a stuck turn, interrupt it and resubmit after the chat is idle. Terminal worktree creation and direct PR links can avoid the affected operations where appropriate.

The sample is limited to the three named tools and retained logs from one day. Raw conversations, private repository details, hostnames, and extracted application bundles are omitted.

items.body:
### Environment

Observed on 22 October 2026.

- Windows 11 Professional, build 10.0.26300, x64 (from the local doctor report).
- Installed desktop package: OpenAI.Codex 26.1016.8120.0.
- Bundled CLI: 0.163.0-alpha.11.1.
- Bundled Windows Computer Use skill: 26.1016.61520; @oai/sky: 0.7.12.
- Classic desktop Outlook is running. A later successful probe from normal interactive PowerShell returned Outlook.Version = 16.0.0.19725.

### Observed behavior

The user needs background access to the existing desktop Outlook session while continuing to use the mouse and keyboard.

Read-only connection probes from the Windows execution context fail:

1. In Windows PowerShell 5.1:
   `[Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::GetActiveObject('Outlook.Application')`
   returns `0x800401E3 (MK_E_UNAVAILABLE)`.

2. In the task's PowerShell:
   `New-Object -ComObject Outlook.Application`
   fails to obtain the Outlook.Application COM class factory with `0x80070005 (E_ACCESSDENIED)`.

The command process has Low mandatory integrity (S-1-16-4096); the Administrators group is deny-only. Its visible process inventory contains only the isolated shell and console host. These observations describe the execution context; they do not establish which specific access check rejects the COM call.

The owner subsequently ran the same New-Object COM connection probe from normal interactive Windows PowerShell outside the task. It succeeded and returned `OK: Outlook 16.0.0.19725`. The result was independently read from the saved diagnostic output as well as the owner's screenshot. This establishes a working COM activation/version query in the interactive context and a failing activation in the restricted task context; it does not identify the exact denying access check or verify all mailbox operations. No registry/COM/security permission repair is claimed.

### Separate launch failure that recovered

Initially, the supported `@oai/sky` import succeeded, but `sky.list_apps()` returned:

`failed to launch codex app-server: program not found`

The configured per-user bundled codex.exe existed and ran by its absolute path, but its directory was absent from the saved User PATH. After adding that actual CLI directory to User PATH and fully terminating/reopening the desktop app:

- the task can resolve `codex` by name;
- `sky.list_apps()` succeeds and detects classic Outlook;
- the direct background COM probes above still fail.

This is a before/after observation for this installation, not proof that all occurrences have the same cause. Related launch report: #51867.

A subsequent UI inspection was interrupted by the user's physical Escape key. UI screenshot/input functionality is therefore not presented as fully verified.

### Requested guidance / diagnostics

Please clarify whether attaching to the existing Outlook COM session is supported from this restricted Windows execution route, and provide a supported background integration or recovery path if available. The user specifically needs an approach that leaves desktop input free.

If this isolation boundary intentionally prevents COM access, please make that limitation and the supported alternative actionable in the product. If access is expected to work, diagnostics identifying the failed COM activation/binding boundary would help.

The exact cause, any relationship between the launch and COM failures, and whether this is a product regression remain unconfirmed. The local doctor report's installation, network, and database integrity checks pass outside the task.

Submitted with the account owner's authorization and AI assistance. This report contains technical versions and minimal probe results only.

### Controlled comparison completed

| Probe | Normal interactive Windows PowerShell | Restricted task PowerShell |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `New-Object -ComObject Outlook.Application`, then `.Version` | Succeeds: `16.0.0.19725` | Activation fails: `0x80070005 E_ACCESSDENIED` |

Please focus follow-up guidance on the supported execution/authorization boundary for background COM, rather than assuming an Outlook installation failure. No attempt was made to evade the task isolation or create an out-of-sandbox execution bridge.


### Historical working-route comparison verified from local session records

Read-only inspection of the owner's local session records from 20 October 2026 found successful direct Outlook COM connection/account enumeration using `New-Object -ComObject Outlook.Application`, with command exit code 0. These were local desktop sessions (originator `codex_work_desktop`) using CLI 0.162.0-alpha.17.2. Their recorded permission state was:

- `sandbox_policy.type = danger-full-access`
- `permission_profile.type = disabled`
- `approval_policy = never`

By contrast, the currently affected Work conversation receives a managed restricted workspace-write execution profile and cannot request sandbox escalation. Its COM activation fails with E_ACCESSDENIED as described above.

The app's saved **local** mode is still `full-access` (`agent-mode-by-host-id.local` and `permission-selection-by-host-id:local.agentMode`). This saved local default must not be confused with the affected conversation's effective permissions. Startup logs also show other local threads resuming with full-access profiles. This is not proof that the current conversation is incorrectly configured, or that it should override any enforced policy.

Please clarify the supported way to select the appropriate local execution route and inspect the effective permissions for this conversation type. The exact reason for the difference in effective policy remains unknown. No local settings, enforced policies, or execution boundaries were bypassed or modified during this comparison. No private session identifiers, paths, mailbox contents, or raw records are attached.

items.body:
## Summary

An existing Codex Desktop thread became unusable after switching from a third-party GLM model through CC Switch back to direct OpenAI access with ChatGPT sign-in. Changing the selected model and fully restarting did not recover it.

Two failures appeared sequentially: a stale third-party model error during remote compaction, then a schema error caused by plaintext reasoning items in the persisted history. After backing up and repairing the affected metadata, and removing only the incompatible reasoning records, the same thread resumed successfully. A subsequent successful compaction was recorded.

## Environment

- Windows; Codex Desktop using ChatGPT sign-in.
- Runtime reported in a newly created session: `0.163.0-alpha.11.1`.
- Affected thread was originally created with runtime `0.160.1`.
- CC Switch installed version at diagnosis: `4.0.18` (the version used for every earlier turn was not independently verified).
- Third-party model: `ccs-zhipu/glm-5.3`.
- Official model selected when diagnosing: `gpt-5.6-sol`; a separate new official-model thread worked.

## Reproduction path observed

1. Continue a long existing thread using GLM through CC Switch.
2. Switch CC Switch back to direct official access with ChatGPT authentication.
3. Select an official model in the affected thread and fully restart Codex.
4. Send another message. Remote compaction fails before a normal reply.
5. After correcting the stale model metadata, retry: remote compaction now fails on persisted reasoning content.

This is an observed recovery case, not a fresh minimal reproduction against a mock provider.

## Errors

First:
```
Error running remote compact task:
The 'ccs-zhipu/glm-5.3' model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account.
```

After the metadata repair:
```
Invalid 'input[30].content': array too long. Expected an array with maximum length 0, but got an array with length 1 instead.
```
The second response was HTTP 400, `invalid_request_error`, code `array_above_max_length`.

## Persisted-history findings

- The thread database already had `model_provider = "openai"` and `model = "gpt-5.6-sol"`.
- Global configuration no longer selected the third-party model or proxy.
- Five historical `turn_context` records and one `world_state` record still contained GLM model fields (including nested model settings).
- After the last pre-failure compaction, 264 `response_item` records had this structural shape (text and identifiers intentionally omitted):

```json
{
  "type": "reasoning",
  "summary": [],
  "content": [{"type": "reasoning_text", "text": "<omitted>"}],
  "encrypted_content": null
}
```

The raw wire request was not captured, so the exact mapping of `input[30]` to a stored item is not proven. However, removing this class of records was the final change that restored the thread.

## Recovery verified locally

With complete backups:
1. Changed only stale GLM `model` fields inside those six historical state/context records to the selected official model. This exposed the second error.
2. Removed the 264 plaintext reasoning response records after the last compaction boundary, leaving all other JSONL records byte-for-byte unchanged.
3. Reloaded the thread. The user confirmed recovery, and a new successful compaction was recorded on 2026-10-22.

User messages, assistant messages, tool calls and tool outputs were retained. No database edits were made. This describes a diagnostic workaround, not a recommendation to modify live session files.

## Expected behavior / requested investigation

Provider/model changes should not permanently wedge an existing thread. Please consider validating history against the destination provider before remote compaction and providing a supported recovery path for incompatible third-party reasoning items. Ideally, preserve useful conversation/tool history and clearly explain any reasoning data that must be excluded.

The responsible serialization layer has not been established; this may require coordination with the proxy.

## Related

- https://github.com/farion1231/cc-switch/issues/8655 — similar stale-model failure after returning to direct official access.
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/36704 — related schema-error symptom, but a different reported migration/recovery scenario.

No full conversation, local paths, account identifiers, credentials or raw reasoning text are included.

items.body:
Add managed network review domains before allow rules

## Why

Managed network policies need to require approval for selected hosts even when an exact or wildcard allow rule matches them.

## What changed

- Add `experimental_network.review_domains` to managed requirements and route matching hosts through the existing network approval flow. Explicit denials retain precedence, and approved connections still undergo DNS and local-address checks.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.40934

### What subscription do you have?

Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

### Description

The ChatGPT Windows desktop application repeatedly displayed the following error when using Work (Codex) mode:

```text
Reconnecting... waiting for network
Reconnecting 1/5
...
Reconnecting 5/5
```

Work sessions were unable to proceed, while regular ChatGPT conversations continued working normally.

### Environment

- Operating system: Windows
- Application: ChatGPT Windows Desktop / Codex Work
- Network proxy: Clash Verge Rev
- Proxy modes tested: TUN + Rule and TUN + Global
- Local HTTP/Mixed proxy port: 7897

### Observed Behavior

1. Regular ChatGPT conversations worked normally.
2. Work mode repeatedly failed to maintain a connection.
3. Switching from Rule to Global mode did not resolve the problem.
4. Disabling MCP integrations did not resolve the problem.
5. The issue disappeared after explicitly configuring proxy environment variables for Codex.

### Network Diagnostics

The local proxy port was listening successfully.

A request through the local HTTP proxy returned:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
```

Additional HTTPS tests returned:

```text
chatgpt.com: 403
www.openai.com: 308
```

These results demonstrated that the proxy tunnel could be established. However, the HTTP 403 response alone does not prove that the proxy caused the Work connection failure.

### Expected Behavior

Work mode should establish and maintain a stable connection when the system's network traffic is routed through a functioning proxy, or provide a clear diagnostic error when additional proxy configuration is required.

### Actual Behavior

Work repeatedly displayed generic network reconnection errors and could not complete tasks, despite regular ChatGPT conversations functioning correctly.

### Resolution

The issue was resolved after explicitly configuring HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY, and NO_PROXY in the Codex environment file and restarting the application.

This suggests a possible proxy configuration inheritance or network routing issue in the Windows Work/Codex runtime. The exact root cause has not been independently confirmed through internal logs.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Launch Clash Verge Rev on Windows.
2. Enable TUN mode and use a working proxy node.
3. Select Rule mode or Global mode.
4. Launch the ChatGPT Windows desktop application without explicitly setting proxy environment variables in the Codex environment file.
5. Verify that ordinary ChatGPT conversations work.
6. Start a new Work (Codex) session.
7. Submit a simple prompt, such as:

   `Hello, please reply with "Connection test successful".`

8. Observe that Work mode repeatedly displays:

   `Reconnecting... waiting for network`

9. Wait until the reconnection attempts reach 5/5.

### Workaround That Resolved the Issue

1. Open the Codex environment file:

   `~/.codex/.env`

2. Add the following configuration, using the local Clash HTTP/Mixed proxy port:

   ```dotenv
   HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7897
   HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7897
   ALL_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7897
   NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1
   ```

3. Save the file.
4. Completely exit and restart the ChatGPT Windows application.
5. Start a new Work session.

**Result:** Work mode resumed functioning normally.

### Additional Notes

- No custom `openai_base_url` or `model_provider` override was found in `config.toml`.
- Temporarily disabling MCP integrations did not resolve the issue.
- WinHTTP reported `Direct access (no proxy server)`, which is not necessarily abnormal when Clash TUN is enabled.
- A direct-network comparison was not possible because ChatGPT was inaccessible without Clash in this environment.
- Reproduction has been confirmed in one local Windows environment; broader reproducibility is unknown.
- No session IDs or internal logs are included to avoid exposing potentially sensitive information.

### What is the expected behavior?

The ChatGPT Windows Work (Codex) mode should establish and maintain a stable connection when the system is using a properly configured network proxy, including Clash Verge Rev with TUN mode enabled.

Specifically:

1. Work mode should function normally when regular ChatGPT conversations can successfully access the service through the same network environment.
2. The Codex runtime should correctly detect and use supported proxy configurations, or clearly document when explicit proxy environment variables are required.
3. Work sessions should execute tasks without repeatedly displaying "Reconnecting... waiting for network".
4. If a connection fails, the application should display a meaningful diagnostic message identifying the likely cause, such as a proxy configuration error or WebSocket connection failure.

Ideally, users should not need to manually configure HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY in the Codex environment file when the operating system is already routing traffic through a functioning proxy.

### Additional information

### Important Finding: Explicit Proxy Configuration Resolved the Issue

The most significant finding is that the issue was resolved by explicitly configuring proxy environment variables in the Codex environment file.

Configuration file:

`~/.codex/.env`

Working configuration:

```dotenv
HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7897
HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7897
ALL_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7897
NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1
```

After completely restarting the ChatGPT Windows application, Work mode began functioning normally.

### Additional Observations

- The issue occurred under both Clash TUN + Rule and TUN + Global modes.
- Regular ChatGPT conversations continued working throughout the incident.
- Disabling MCP integrations did not resolve the problem.
- No custom OpenAI API endpoint was configured in `config.toml`.
- The local HTTP proxy was listening and could establish HTTPS tunnels.
- The Windows WinHTTP proxy was configured for direct access.
- Direct connectivity without Clash could not be tested in this environment.

### Possible Root Cause

This behavior suggests that the Windows Work/Codex runtime may not consistently use the intended proxy configuration when relying solely on system-level TUN routing.

Explicitly setting the proxy environment variables resolved the problem in my environment, although the exact internal failure mechanism has not been verified through logs.

### Suggested Improvement

It would be helpful if the application could:

1. Automatically detect supported Windows proxy configurations more reliably.
2. Provide a built-in proxy configuration option for Work mode.
3. Display more specific diagnostic information when WebSocket or proxy connections fail.
4. Document the relationship between Windows system proxy settings, TUN routing, and Codex proxy environment variables.

This workaround may be useful to other Windows users experiencing similar reconnection issues.

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: app

labels.name: app-server

items.body:
## Request

Please expose an atomic conditional resume operation for an **existing** goal. A user-authorized scheduled recovery should be able to resume a mistakenly blocked continuing mission without overwriting a concurrent manual pause, replacing the objective, resetting usage, or changing its budget.

The installed desktop build21161 protocol schema exposes `thread/goal/set` with `threadId`, `origin`, `objective`, `status`, and `tokenBudget`. The current public [ThreadGoalSetParams](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs) and [request processor](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_goal_processor.rs) do not provide an expected status/revision parameter. The returned goal has timestamps, but no opaque revision token.

## Why client rereads are insufficient

This is a protocol race derived from the schema/source, not a claim that we overwrote a real user's pause:

1. Recovery client reads existing goalG as blocked.
2. A user pauses G in the desktop client.
3. Recovery client sends `thread/goal/set` with statusactive based on its earlier observation.

Repeated client-side checks narrow this window but cannot make the final write conditional. In our local prototype, an isolated fake-client probe also caught an avoidable disk-checkpoint gap; we fixed it by rereading after the durable checkpoint. That repair still cannot eliminate the final API race. We have not intentionally paused/resumed a production goal to demonstrate it.

## Suggested contract

Either a dedicated conditional resume method or optional preconditions on `thread/goal/set`:

- expected existing goal identity and an opaque monotonic revision;
- expected current statusblocked;
- truthful automatic mutation provenance, preserving all normal permission and writer-ownership rules;
- atomic check and status update across clients/processes;
- a stale precondition returns a conflict/no-op with no lifecycle mutation.

Do not make automatic callers impersonate an explicit user action, bypass live-writer protections, or switch to direct database changes. Goal creation, clear, objective replacement, budget changes and quota resets are outside this request.

## Acceptance examples

- Unchanged enrolled blocked goal plus valid preconditions can resume, preserving objective, identity, usage and budget.
- A concurrent pause, completion, clear/replacement or limit state causes the stale resume to fail without changing that newer state.
- Two updates in the same timestamp second still have distinct revisions.
- An acknowledgement alone is not work continuation: clients still need normal native turn/progress evidence.

This would support bounded recovery policies, not a promise that goals can never legitimately block or stop. A genuine full-work blocker, explicit stop, approval, CAPTCHA or OAuth boundary must remain effective. If an equivalent supported operation already exists, please point us to its public contract.

### What variant of Codex are you using?

App

### What feature would you like to see?

[Feature Request] Independent Context & Memory Editor with AI-Assisted Optimization and Session Recovery

Product: Codex Desktop App
Category: Enhancement / Context Management

Summary

Introduce an independent Context & Memory Editor that allows developers to selectively remove, compress, preserve, and restore conversation context without restarting their Codex sessions.

The editor would operate in a separate window with its own AI assistant and include a one-click Optimize Context feature.

The Problem

During long development sessions, Codex accumulates information from experiments, debugging, code analysis, images, and tool outputs. Much of this information eventually becomes irrelevant.

Current compaction mechanisms provide limited control over which information is preserved.

I have repeatedly encountered:

{"error":"decompressed request body exceeds 67108864 bytes"}

This occurred while Codex still reported 29% of its context window remaining.

Because these errors occur during active operations, users cannot reliably anticipate them. Restarting conversations also disrupts development workflows.

Proposed Solution

1. Independent Context & Memory Editor

A separate window with its own AI chat, independent of the main Codex conversation.

Users can inspect context grouped by tasks, experiments, and conversation segments.

Each segment supports three actions:

* REMOVE: Exclude information from future model requests while keeping it recoverable.
* COMPRESS: Replace information with concise, user-editable summaries.
* KEEP ACTIVE: Preserve information in full detail.

Example:
“Remove experiments 1 and 2, compress experiments 3 and 4, and keep experiment 5 fully active.”

These operations must actually change the context transmitted in subsequent requests, not merely instruct Codex to ignore information.

2. Optimize Context Button

A prominent Optimize Context button, accessible directly from the main Codex conversation, opens the independent editor.

The AI assistant would:

1. Identify obsolete experiments, redundant information, and oversized tool outputs.
2. Recommend which segments to remove, compress, or preserve.
3. Estimate token and request-size savings.
4. Present editable summaries and proposed changes.
5. Apply changes only after user approval.

Users retain full control. No context is discarded or compressed without confirmation.

3. Independent, Bounded AI Context

The Memory Editor must not inherit the entire conversation history.

Instead, it should use a structured context index and retrieve only the segments required for each operation.

Large segments should be processed incrementally. Each editing task should use bounded temporary context, preventing the Memory Editor itself from becoming overloaded.

4. Proactive Warnings & Session Recovery

Codex should warn users when context usage or request payload size approaches critical limits.

Example:

“Context usage is increasing. Would you like to optimize your context?”

[Optimize Context] [Continue Working]

If the main conversation fails because of context or request-size limits, the Memory Editor must remain accessible.

Users should be able to optimize the active context and resume the existing conversation without restarting it.

5. Additional Features

* Visual overview of active context and estimated token usage.
* Separate indicators for model context and request payload size.
* Editable compression summaries.
* Undo and recovery of removed context.
* Separation of session context and persistent project memory.
* Context optimization without restarting the conversation.

Related Feature Requests

Several existing proposals address individual aspects of this problem:

* #33769 – Selective Active-Context Editing
* #36669 – Model-Callable Context Management
* #50320 – Workflow-Aware Adaptive Compaction
* #28860 – Selective Context Transfer
* #50123 – Context Recovery After Failure

This proposal aims to combine these concepts into a unified, user-controlled interface.

The key addition is an independent AI-powered Memory Editor that remains functional even when the main Codex session becomes overloaded.

Expected Benefits

* Longer, uninterrupted development sessions.
* Less irrelevant information consuming context.
* Greater transparency and user control.
* Reduced unnecessary token processing and request payload sizes.
* Recovery from overloaded conversations.
* More efficient management of complex, long-running projects.

Conclusion

As AI coding agents become increasingly autonomous, developers need direct control over their assistants’ working memory.

Developers should decide what their AI remembers, what it summarizes, and what it forgets.

An independent Context & Memory Editor with one-click optimization and session recovery would make Codex more efficient, transparent, and reliable for long-running development projects.
